claims.claim: Identity columns, TRUNCATE TABLE and MERGE (GA) are supported; triggers are not; ALTER COLUMN and nested CTEs are in preview.
PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE are supported only as NONCLUSTERED NOT ENFORCED, FOREIGN KEY only as NOT ENFORCED.

Unsupported types and alternatives: nchar/nvarchar to char/varchar, money to decimal, datetime to datetime2, tinyint to smallint; varchar(max) limited to 16 MB; datetime2 limited to 6 fractional digits.

concept_html:
Fabric Warehouse speaks T-SQL, and most SQL Server habits carry over: CREATE TABLE, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, stored procedures, views, TRUNCATE TABLE, identity columns and explicit transactions. MERGE is generally available. Its tables are Delta tables in OneLake, so Spark and Power BI read them too.

The differences cause real bugs. Microsoft Learn, checked September 2026:

Keys are not enforced. PRIMARY KEY is supported only as NONCLUSTERED NOT ENFORCED. UNIQUE likewise, and FOREIGN KEY only NOT ENFORCED. The engine uses them as hints for query plans. It does not stop duplicates or orphans. Deduplicate and check keys yourself (lesson A3-L1 for MERGE sources, lesson A6-L1 for contracts).

Some data types are missing, with documented alternatives:

Not supported Use
nchar, nvarchar char, varchar (UTF-8 collation)
money, smallmoney decimal
datetime, smalldatetime datetime2 (up to 6 fractional digits)
tinyint smallint
text, ntext, json varchar

varchar(max) is limited to 16 MB per value.

Some features are absent or in preview. Triggers are not supported. ALTER COLUMN and nested CTEs are in preview. Check the T-SQL surface area page before you port a procedure that relies on them.

Porting a SQL Server script is usually a type-mapping job plus one design change: replace constraint enforcement with explicit checks.

lines: CREATE TABLE dbo.dim_customer (
customer_id INT NOT NULL,
name VARCHAR(200),
credit_limit DECIMAL(19, 4),
created_at DATETIME2(6)
ALTER TABLE dbo.dim_customer
ADD CONSTRAINT pk_dim_customer PRIMARY KEY NONCLUSTERED (customer_id) NOT ENFORCED;
-- The key is a hint, so check it after every load.
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

title: Warehouse T-SQL, and where it differs from SQL Server
why_html: A team ported a customer dimension from SQL Server, where PRIMARY KEY had rejected duplicate loads for years. In Fabric the same key was created NOT ENFORCED, so a pipeline that ran twice on the same file loaded every customer twice. Sales per customer halved in the joined reports for a week before anyone traced it. A duplicate check after each load would have failed the run on the first rerun.
